changed.ours: Later I found that some of the uselessness was built-in due to the monastic rules. The Vinaya, the code of conduct for Theravāda Buddhist monastics – in the oldest surviving Buddhist sect – includes Pācittiya 8, requiring confession if a monastic tells anyone who isn’t fully ordained (a layperson or a novice, say) about a genuine “superior human state,” including meditative absorption, psychic knowledge, or a path or fruit of awakening (a stage of enlightenment). A false attainment claim brings Pārājika 4, permanent expulsion from the order. So CYA applies to anyone with status to protect: monastic authors have an excellent reason to repeat lists and techniques while staying maddeningly vague about their own experience. Literal translations are narrower and actually clearer, explaining how to take apart or empty out our crude idea of “things,” though they still don’t get to my parallel-flows understanding (each sense as its own flow, with no self between them). changed.ours: You don’t need several sense streams working together to suffer; one stream is enough. Say all that was left was a single channel of pleasure and pain. Pain would still be in there, because pain is like a plane: it can only land if there’s somewhere solid to land, and even one channel gives it that. During full unweaving, no assembled system remains that could suffer, lack, desire, gain, lose, recognize, or do anything. Supreme bliss is what seems to be left when the capacity for suffering is released (even though you might assume neutrality would be left): as Sāriputta put it in AN 9.34, “nibbāna is pleasant precisely where nothing is felt.”

But many people remain confused about whether he denied a self or merely denied that conditioned experience is the true self. In one of the most quoted suttas, SN 44.10, he refuses to answer the question directly because either answer would confuse an already confused person further. But in many other suttas he specifically states that self-view itself is the problem, and the self is just composed of changing aggregates.

So if someone still needed a second, later event before that realization arrived, then the first event wasn’t stream-entry fruition, by the very meaning of the term. The early Pāli texts do give us some very similar kind of symbolism, though. And Dhammapada 170 asks us to see the world as a bubble and mirage, so if you put it all together, you can certainly imagine that the basic idea of life being like a dream was originally intended.

changed.ours: Stream entry’s greatest prize is a “release date”: AN 3.88 allows at most seven more lives before final awakening. There is actually quite a lot of modern academic evidence for rebirth. But who’s going around getting reborn if no permanent self exists? Buddhists don’t imagine any permanent self-essence/soul moving between bodies. Rather, rebirth is seen as a causal process: there is a continuity (often called a “mind-stream”), but there is not a “thing” that’s moving from one life to the next. Craving and clinging lead to becoming, and becoming leads to birth. More like a driverless car. The later Buddhist philosopher Milindapañha compared rebirth to one lamp being used to lighting another.
